overreach: Changes in automotive radar mainly push oscilloscopes from “simple time-domain probing” toward wideband, high-speed, multi-channel, phase-coherent, deep-memory measurement platforms
Modern automotive radar has moved from narrowband 24 GHz systems toward 76–81 GHz radar with several GHz of RF sweep bandwidth
Required oscilloscope capability increases in: analog bandwidth, sampling rate, low noise floor, high effective number of bits
Shorter chirp duration and steeper frequency ramps require the oscilloscope to capture fast transient behavior, ramp linearity errors, PLL settling, glitches, and phase discontinuities
Radar waveforms are no longer only simple linear chirps; systems may use advanced modulation, interference mitigation, coding, or adaptive waveforms
MIMO and cascaded radar chips → more oscilloscope channels and synchronization
Radar ICs combine RF, PLLs, ADCs, digital interfaces, power management, and high-speed data links
Automotive safety and production pressure → repeatable automated measurements
review.reason: The cited passage only supports that the FSW-B2071 option records I/Q data using supported R&S RTO oscilloscopes with the RTO-B4 option to obtain specified performance. The answer makes broad claims about automotive radar evolution, FMCW chirps, MIMO, SoCs, bandwidth, synchronization, memory, automation, and safety/production requirements that are not evidenced by the passage.
